candidates.sentence: Multiple imputation treats missing data through a division of labor that has served applied research for nearly four decades: an imputer fills in the missing values several times from a model for the complete data, an analyst fits the model of substantive interest to each completed data set, and simple rules combine the results .

Reviews of the field's state of the art describe a mature methodology , in which the role of the missing-data mechanism is understood, point estimates recover their complete-data targets under stated conditions, and Wald-type tests for single and multiple parameters are well calibrated.

Only one information criterion has been proposed specifically for averaging over multiply imputed data, and its authors call for further theoretical and practical study of the method while placing that work beyond their own scope .

The applied guides are silent on the same question: the standard book-length treatment does not treat information criteria for multiply imputed data at all , and neither does the current state-of-the-art review .

We propose a standard, the *complete-data replication principle*, and organize this paper around it: a procedure for multiply imputed data replicates complete-data inference when, on average over repeated samples, it reaches the same conclusion that would have been reached had no data been missing.
At the first level, estimates recover their complete-data targets; this is the classical level, and Rubin's rules settle it.
At the second level, the decision criterion itself (a deviance or an information criterion) recovers its complete-data counterpart in expectation.
At the third level, decision rates match: the same model is selected, and the same hypotheses are rejected, as often as they would have been with complete data.

Stated this way, the settled results are settled because they pass at the first level, and posing the second and third levels reframes the open questions, which had been posed only at the first level.

Benchmarking selection methods against the full data is not new in itself, because simulation comparisons of that kind appear in and ; the principle as an explicit yardstick is, to our knowledge, stated here for the first time, and we add a characterization of when it can and cannot be met.
The obstacle is a bias in the averaged log-likelihood, and this paper's central result describes the leading term of that bias exactly.

When a likelihood model with an estimated variance or covariance is fit to congenially imputed data, we show that the averaged log-likelihood overstates its complete-data counterpart by The first term, one half the trace of the relative-increase-in-variance matrix (a standard object in the MI literature), adds up the missing information about the model's parameters; the second, smaller term reflects imbalance between the observed and the missing units on the conditioning variables, and vanishes when the data are missing completely at random.
The practical consequence is that, for such a model, every deviance and information criterion built on the averaged log-likelihood across imputations is, in expectation, too optimistic.

The more serious consequence is that the optimism is not uniform across models: because each candidate's criterion is inflated in proportion to that candidate's own missing information, a model-comparison table built on imputed data tends, all else equal, to favor the candidates with the most missing information, and in our pre-registered simulations 100% of uncorrected MI-AIC's misclassifications fell on the candidate with the largest RIV.
Adding each candidate's own trace back to its criterion recovers, as we show, the criterion's complete-data expectation at any signal strength, so the principle's second level is met in full.
The principle's third level asks for more: the same decisions at the same rates as the complete data.

In the first, the competing models fit equally well, in the sense that the smaller model is true, and correction then restores complete-data behavior: calibrated tests reject at the complete-data rate , and selection that matches the criterion's full null distribution chooses models indistinguishably from complete-data AIC in our pre-registered design.

The missing data have then destroyed part of the evidence in its favor, and the corrected criteria and calibrated tests studied here cannot recover it; the relevant statistics shrink by factors we predict, and the remaining shortfall is information loss rather than a fixable calibration error.

As a penalty the correction is precedented, because it reproduces <math> of , the criterion that halved the missing-data surcharge of the earlier complete-data-discrepancy criteria ; all of those criteria were derived for deterministic EM estimation under a fixed missingness pattern.

Two other routes deserve mention: the missing-covariate criteria of target a different, Takeuchi-type discrepancy, and the reweighting route of reaches the complete-data target through inverse-probability weights but explicitly leaves an imputation-based criterion open.
Fourth is the closed-form leading-order differential bias of the likelihood-ratio numerator at the null in the complete-data metric.
Congeniality is assumed throughout , and the bias derived here is what remains after the imputer and the analyst agree.

**A correction for model selection after imputation.** Choosing among models by AIC or BIC on multiply imputed data is biased, and the bias is specific to each candidate and grows with that candidate's missing information.

Adding one term per candidate, the trace of its relative-increase-in-variance matrix, removes the trace component of the bias and substantially restores the ranking that complete data would have given.

**The deviance bias behind the correction.** For a model that estimates a scale or covariance, we show that the averaged log-likelihood across imputations overstates its complete-data counterpart by half the trace of the relative-increase-in-variance matrix, plus a design-imbalance term that appears only under data missing at random and disappears when data are missing completely at random.

**The bias of a likelihood-ratio comparison.** For two nested models compared at the null, the relevant bias is the missing information carried by the tested directions alone, measured in the complete-data metric.
The obvious alternative, the difference of the two models' separate corrections, always overstates it.
**A sharper way to run that comparison.** Fitting the competing models to the same imputed data sets rather than to separate ones cancels most of the shared noise and tightens the comparison.
